summary: Examines a possible lockup, or deadlock, in the IMP subnet caused by message sequencing. It explains that protocols must be designed carefully to avoid lockups, which usually show up only in unforeseen circumstances.

plainLanguage.summary: A traffic jam where everyone waits for someone else could freeze the network. This paper explains how that could happen.

subtitle: How message ordering in the ARPANET could cause a traffic jam.

tldr.problem: When the ARPANET added message sequencing to prevent one kind of deadlock, it accidentally created the risk of another: messages waiting in order could consume all buffer space, freezing the network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a scenario where single-packet and multi-packet messages competing for the same buffers can form a cycle of dependencies, leaving no buffers free for the messages that must go first.
tldr.outcome: The paper proposes reserving at least one buffer exclusively for single-packet messages to break the deadlock cycle, a simple fix that protects against a subtle failure mode.

today: The ARPANET eventually corrected this issue by improving its flow control. The lessons from detecting subtle deadlocks in early packet-switched networks continue to guide protocol design.

sections.title: Deadlock in the ARPANET
sections.content: Deadlock or lockup is when all parts of a system wait for each other and nothing can proceed. The ARPANET had seen deadlocks before, most notably the "Christmas lockup" of 1973, when snapshot messages filled all reassembly buffers. The RFC examines a new risk introduced by message sequencing: a potential deadlock that has not yet occurred but could emerge as traffic grows.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes computers get stuck waiting for each other, and nothing happens. This paper warns of a new way the ARPANET could get stuck.

sections.title: The Sequencing Problem
sections.content: Messages are numbered to preserve order: they must leave a destination in the same order they entered the source. To prevent deadlock, the IMPSYS (the switching software) will only give buffer allocation to the next message in sequence; messages out of order are treated as buffer requests and discarded. However, buffer allocations piggy-backed on acknowledgments (RFNMs) go to the next multi-packet message, not the next message in sequence. If the next message in sequence is a single-packet message waiting for a buffer, all available buffers can be claimed by out-of-order multi-packet messages, creating a circular dependency.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages get numbers to stay in order. But the system can accidentally give buffers to the wrong messages, trapping the ones that must go first.

sections.title: The Fix
sections.content: The proposed solution is to reserve at least one reassembly buffer (or one per destination) for use only by single-packet messages. This ensures that even in the worst case, the next message in sequence can always be accepted, breaking the deadlock cycle. The RFC notes that moving sequencing from the IMP level to the HOST level might also help, but that would require coordinating changes across many different computers on the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep one special buffer just for small messages so they never run out of space, and bigger messages can't hog everything.

references.text: Kahn, R. E. and W. R. Crowther, "Flow Control in a Resource-Sharing Computer Network," IEEE Transactions on Communication, June 1972.
